name: Hakata Station
label: Hakata Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '東7番街屋上庭園' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '西07' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3637038754: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hakata'.
notes: Major rail hub with a rooftop garden and the Kitte Hakata plaza.

text.description:
Hakata Station is the largest and busiest railway terminal in Kyushu, and the place where the Shinkansen from Osaka finally stops. For a phone photographer, the building works best as a bold city-gateway scene rather than a single tidy facade. It has big glass and stone shapes, glowing lights in the evening, and a constant flow of people and trains.

The station was rebuilt in 2011. The JR Hakata City complex opened on 3 March 2011, and the Kyushu Shinkansen services began nine days later. The very first station here opened in 1889, about 600 m north of where it stands today. In the last full fiscal year, an average of 125,462 people boarded here each day, so expect a lively scene.

For a calmer and more interesting view, head up to the rooftop garden 東7番街屋上庭園 in the station area. From there you look down on the station district at a slightly different angle. The illuminated, Hakata-coloured wall of the building is visible from above, and the height lets you compress the city streets into a layered picture. If you have time, the rooftop square つばめの杜ひろば gives a wider panorama, with trains arriving and leaving below.

Keep your phone steady against a railing, avoid including other people's faces in close-up, and take a few frames at different zoom levels before you move on.
text.geographic_location: Hakata Station is in Hakata-ku, Fukuoka, and is the city's main rail hub. The rooftop garden is a nearby elevated viewpoint that may be on Amu Plaza's 11th floor, so check on the day.
text.directions_text: Hakata Station is served by JR trains, the Shinkansen and the Fukuoka City Subway (Airport Line and Nanakuma Line), so you can arrive right at the station. Check the official site before you go for how to reach the rooftop and when it is open. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to compress the station district and pick out the lit wall. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider view of the streets, and keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for close-up details, since it can make the buildings lean and look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 東7番街屋上庭園 (rooftop garden, Hakata Station area). An elevated, slightly different angle over the station area, with the illuminated Hakata-coloured wall of the building visible from above, suited to telephoto compression of the city. It is a quieter, slightly different elevated angle than the main terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Zoom in so the lit wall and the surrounding rooftops fill the frame, layering the city behind it. Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon of rooftops up with the top third of the picture. If you want a wider panorama with trains below, the rooftop square つばめの杜ひろば is a good second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall or building you want sharp, then slide the exposure down slightly so the lights do not burn out. Rest your elbows on a railing to keep the telephoto frame steady, and switch on night mode after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening, when the building's lighting is on and the sky still has some colour, should give the most atmospheric results.

text.access_note: Rooftop areas and station facilities can have set opening times and entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Canal City Hakata
label: Canal City Hakata
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Canal City Hakata'.
notes: Shopping and entertainment complex with a fountain show.

text.description:
Canal City Hakata is a large shopping and entertainment complex in Fukuoka, often called "the city within the city". Shops, cafes, restaurants, cinemas, a theatre, a game centre and two hotels sit around a canal that runs right through the middle. It photographs well because the buildings are anything but boxy. The Jerde Partnership designed it in a fanciful style, with curving sculptures and fountains, and the surrounding city is hardly visible from inside. That gives your pictures a self-contained, almost stage-set feel.

Some facts to put it in context. It opened on 20 April 1996 and cost about $1.4 billion, making it the largest private development in Japan's history. For its 20th anniversary in 2016 it added the "Aqua Panorama" fountain and staged Japan's largest 3D projection mapping. In 2001 the Ramen Stadium arrived, with several of Fukuoka's well-known ramen restaurants.

For photos, think in layers: the curved facades, the water of the canal, and the people walking past give you depth and scale. Keep to the open walkways and avoid blocking the flow of shoppers. If a fountain display is running, a short video or a Live Photo will capture it better than a still. Display times change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Canal City Hakata is in the Hakata area of Fukuoka, next to the city's entertainment district and between its commercial and retail core.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the phone icon on the map. It is about 159 m south of the complex, which is about 3 minutes on foot, so head north from there. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the sweep of the curving buildings and the canal. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out sculptures, signs and fountain details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. It is roughly 3 minutes on foot from there to the complex itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the canal or a curved edge of the building along one of the lines, so the shape leads the eye into the picture. Include a few people for scale. Then move closer and shoot upwards with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to exaggerate the curves.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the brightest part of the building, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so lights and screens do not wash out. If a fountain show is running, try a Live Photo or a short video. After dark, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a rail or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening, when the lighting comes on, tends to suit the colourful design and the water. Daytime is better for clean views of the shapes without crowds of lights competing.

text.access_note: This is a shopping and entertainment complex with public walkways, but opening times and events vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ōhori Park
label: Ohori Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '浮見堂' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '浮見堂' (way/210616055): middle (8 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23344558: large area 'Ōhori Park' (1094 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large pond park with bridges and walking paths.

text.description:
Ōhori Park is a big city park built around a lake, and it is one of the easiest places in Fukuoka to take a relaxed, good-looking phone photo. The name means "large moat": the lake began as part of the moat for Fukuoka Castle, made by the lord Kuroda Nagamasa from the northern half of an old inlet. The present park was laid out by Fukuoka City, modelled on the West Lake of China, and opened in 1929. A fireworks festival is held here every August.

The picture most visitors come for is the red-and-green pavilion, 浮見堂 (Ukimido), standing over the water on the central island. Guides call it the park's symbol. It works well because the bright pavilion is reflected in the lake, with trees and the city skyline behind it. You reach it over the bridges, so the walk to the viewpoint is part of the fun.

If you want a second angle, the lake and the pavilion can also be seen from the bridge 観月橋. At dusk the water turns blue and the park lights come on, which gives a calmer, moodier shot. The path around the lake is busy with walkers, joggers and dogs, so keep an eye out when you are composing a photo. The Fukuoka Art Museum is close by if you want to combine the two.
text.geographic_location: Ōhori Park is in Chūō-ku, in central Fukuoka, on the site of a former cove that opened onto Hakata Bay. The Fukuoka Art Museum is nearby.
text.directions_text: Ōhori Park is in Chūō-ku, so head for the Chūō-ku area of central Fukuoka. Check a map for your route. Once inside, follow the paths and bridges to the central island, where the pavilion stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pavilion and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole lake and sky from the bridges. Use 2x if you want to pick out the pavilion from across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the central island, in front of the pavilion, approached over the bridges). The red-and-green pavilion standing over the lake, with its reflection on the water and the city and trees behind it. The best view for this spot is in front of 浮見堂 (Ukimido), on the central island, which you reach over the bridges.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a line. Keep the pavilion off-centre and let its reflection fill the lower part of the frame. Hold the phone low and close to the water for a stronger reflection. For an alternative view, try the bridge 観月橋, which looks across the lake to the pavilion, but check it on the ground. Wait a moment for walkers and joggers to pass before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the red stays rich and the sky does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing, as the lights come on and the water turns blue.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the water is calmest, according to one guide. Dusk is another option, when the lake turns blue and the park lights come on.

text.access_note: The park itself is an open public space, but the Japanese garden may charge an entry fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kushida Shrine
label: Kushida Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '大手筋通り' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '那の津通り' (way/163537331): point nearest the subject (169 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45779975: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kushida Shrine' (176 m across).
notes: Hakata's guardian shrine, home of the Gion Yamakasa festival floats.

text.description: Kushida Shrine is a Shinto shrine in Hakata-ku, Fukuoka. It is dedicated to Amaterasu and Susanoo and is said to have been founded in 757. It is also the centre of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival, which is why a giant festival float is on show here (it is displayed year-round except June, though its position in the grounds may change). It photographs well because it has strong shapes: the main torii, the sweeping roof of the main hall behind it, and an old ginkgo tree with a roped trunk. In late November the ground beneath the ginkgo is covered in yellow leaves. For the shrine itself, shoot upward from the approach so the torii and the roof sit together in one frame. As a quieter alternative near the shrine, try the covered shopping street 大手筋通り, which runs between the Kawabata arcade and the Hakata Riverain building. Old fabric and lacquerware shop fronts, with goods on wooden shelves, make a calm street-photography scene in soft, even light. Photography is restricted inside the main hall and in the lucky-charm and ema areas. Turn your flash off near the main hall and follow any signs. Weekend midday is crowded, so a weekday visit is easier.
text.geographic_location: Kushida Shrine is in Hakata-ku, in the Hakata area of Fukuoka. The covered street 大手筋通り is a separate, quieter suggestion near the shrine.
text.directions_text: From there the shrine lies to the east, about 40 minutes on foot. Follow the walk on your map app. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the shop fronts and for the shrine approach. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof of the main hall or the roped ginkgo trunk. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can stand back far enough to keep the torii upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 大手筋通り (stretch between the Kawabata arcade and the Hakata Riverain building). Old fabric and lacquerware shop fronts with goods on wooden shelves under the covered arcade, lit by soft diffuse light. For the torii and main hall, walk to the shrine and shoot from its approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: In the 大手筋通り arcade, turn on gridlines and line up the shelves and the roofline with them, so the rows of goods look neat. Frame a shop front with a little of the arcade ceiling above it. At the shrine, a second viewpoint is the approach, shooting upward at the main torii with the main hall roof behind it. A third is the ginkgo tree, framed against the shrine buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the shelves to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the lit goods keep their colour. Keep flash off, especially near the main hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The arcade has soft, even light at any hour, so time of day matters little there. At the shrine, a weekday is calmer than a weekend midday, and late November is the time for the yellow ginkgo leaves.

text.access_note: The shrine is a place of worship, and photography is restricted inside the main hall and in the lucky-charm and ema areas, so follow posted signs and check the official site before you go.

name: Fukuoka Tower
label: Fukuoka Tower
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak. Moved 23 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 150 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/772670439: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fukuoka Tower' (32 m across).
notes: Mirrored seaside tower, tallest seaside tower in Japan.

text.description:
Fukuoka Tower is a 234-metre tower in the Momochihama area, built on land reclaimed from Hakata Bay. It is the tallest seaside tower in Japan. It was finished in 1989 after 14 months of building. Its triangular body is covered with about 8000 half-mirrors, which is why it is nicknamed the "Mirror Sail". From outside the glass reflects the sky, so the tower looks different with the weather: pale and silvery on a hazy day, deep blue when it is clear.

That clean, mirrored shape is the reason it works on a phone. It is a simple, tall subject against open sky, with few distractions behind it. The highest observation deck sits at 123 metres, and a 111-metre television mast rises above it. The tower is said to be busiest at sunset, so expect company if you come then.

That is close enough to make it feel huge, but you will need to tilt the phone up to fit it in. Stepping back a little if you can, or using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), helps you keep the whole tower and a good slice of sky in one frame. Keep the phone as upright as you can to stop the sides leaning inward too much. Take a few frames at different times of day, because the mirrored surface changes with the light.
text.geographic_location: Fukuoka Tower stands in the Momochihama area of Sawara-ku, Fukuoka, on reclaimed land beside Hakata Bay.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Momochihama area of Sawara-ku and look for the tower, which is easy to see from a distance. By taxi or hired scooter is the simplest way to get there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and plenty of sky into the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, or try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the mirrored surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in シーサイドももち海浜公園 (Momochi Seaside Park) (ocean side, on the beach directly behind the tower). The full tower exterior rising behind the sandy beach, with sea and sky in the same frame. Choose a spot where nothing blocks the view of the tower's base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone to portrait orientation, switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line. Leave a little space above the top of the mast. If the sides lean inwards, step back or use the default lens (1x) and crop slightly afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the mirrored surface keeps its colour and the sky does not turn white. Use night mode only if the light has dropped, and hold the phone as steady as you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset is the time the tower is most visited, and it gives the mirrored surface plenty of sky colour to reflect. A clear day gives the cleanest, bluest reflection.

text.access_note: The tower grounds and observation decks may have set visiting rules or ticketing, so check the official site before you go.

name: Tōchō-ji
label: Tochoji Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '五重塔' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '五重塔' (way/379033824): middle (19 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/767775372: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tōchō Temple' (173 m across).
notes: Temple with Japan's largest seated wooden Buddha and a five-storey pagoda.

text.description: Tōchō-ji is a Shingon Buddhist temple in the Hakata part of Fukuoka. Tradition says Kūkai founded it in 806, which makes it the oldest Shingon temple on Kyushu. It first stood by the sea. After it burned down at the end of the 16th century, Kuroda Tadayuki, the second lord of Chikuzen, moved it to its present site. For a phone photographer, the draw is the vermilion five-storey wooden pagoda. Seen against blue sky and greenery, its colour stands out clearly, and guides treat it as the temple's signature photo. Cherry trees around it make a popular backdrop in season. The challenge is the city behind the temple. Step to one side in the grounds until the Hakata tower blocks drop out of the frame and only sky and trees sit behind the pagoda. Two other subjects are worth a few frames. One is the hexagonal Rokkaku-dō hall, built in 1842. The other is the temple's heavy gate, which can frame the pagoda or a cherry tree from the street side. The temple also has a 10.8 metre seated Buddha, carved between 1988 and about 1992. Photography is not allowed inside the Great Buddha hall or the main hall, so keep your shots outdoors.
text.geographic_location: Tōchō-ji is in the Hakata area of Fukuoka, a temple precinct with the city's tall buildings rising behind it.
text.directions_text: Head for the Hakata area of Fukuoka to reach Tōchō-ji; no station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Look for the pagoda; it is the easiest landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from a little way back to get the whole pagoda against the sky. If you are close to it, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height in. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda and keep the city buildings out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (shoot from the temple grounds, with the pagoda against the sky; step to one side so the city buildings behind it stay out of frame). The vermilion five-story cypress pagoda standing out against blue sky and greenery, with the Hakata skyscrapers mostly excluded. Look for the pagoda from there and adjust your position, stepping to one side until the city buildings behind it are out of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the pagoda's vertical lines straight by holding the phone upright and level. Leave sky above the top of the roof. For a second picture, frame the Rokkaku-dō hall or use the temple gate to frame the pagoda or a cherry tree from the street side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the vermilion does not wash out. Don't use flash or Night mode indoors; photography is not allowed in the main halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Cherry blossom around the pagoda is popular in season, so check the bloom before you go if that is what you want.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship with some halls where photography is not allowed, so check the official site before you go for opening times and access.

name: Fukuoka Castle
label: Fukuoka Castle ruins
camera_source: Commons cluster (13 photos). Moved 124 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 50 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/345642780: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fukuoka Castle' (538 m across).
notes: Stone walls and turrets of the Edo-period castle, a famed cherry blossom spot.

text.description: Fukuoka Castle sits on top of Fukusaki hill in the middle of the city. Today it is best known for its huge dry-stone walls, old gates and turrets (called yaguras), which are spread through Maizuru Park. There is no need to hunt for one famous angle. You can walk among the stonework and pick your own frames, with grass, trees and old masonry giving you plenty of texture. The castle was finished in 1607 after seven years of building. It is said to have had 47 yaguras and to have covered 47,000 square metres, making it the largest in the Kyūshū region. Its other name, Seki-jō, means 'Stone Castle', and the walls explain why. One of the surviving turrets, the Minamimaru Tamon Yagura, dates from 1854 and is an Important Cultural Property. Beneath the grounds, the remains of an ancient guest house for foreign diplomats were found in 1987. For photos, look for a corner where a wall leads the eye towards a gate or turret, and keep a few trees or branches at the edge of the frame for depth. Stone walls are a good subject for a phone because they are solid and detailed. Go slowly and take a few versions of each view: one wide, one closer, and one with a person standing by the wall for scale. Paths in a park can be uneven, so watch your step while you look at the screen.
text.geographic_location: Fukuoka Castle is in Chūō-ku, in the centre of Fukuoka, on Fukusaki hill. The Naka River runs on the Hakata side to the east, and Ōhori Park lies to the west of the inner castle.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Fukuoka in Chūō-ku and use your preferred map app to head for Maizuru Park, which covers much of the old castle grounds. Hakata is across the Naka River to the east, and Ōhori Park is to the west of the castle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for walls, gates and turrets. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to a long stretch of stonework or want to include the sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details of a turret or the pattern of the stones from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from below the stone wall, looking up at the turret). The turret standing on its high stone wall, framed against the rampart.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the base of a wall on the lower line so it leads the eye up to a gate or turret. Keep the phone level so the walls do not look tilted, and use the ultra-wide only when you have room to step back, as it stretches the edges. For a second view, step back and use telephoto to compress the stonework and the turret.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone or the turret to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it does not wash out. Switch on Live Photos if you like, to catch a moment when people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the texture of the stone and avoids harsh shadows. A quieter time of day also makes it easier to take photos without people in them.

text.access_note: Much of the castle site is now Maizuru Park, but facilities inside may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Low-angle morning or late-afternoon light usually brings out the texture of stone walls.
Quieter times of day usually mean fewer people in photos.
Paths in the park may be uneven in places.
The stand-here point is within the castle grounds, with walls and turrets visible when looking west.

name: Nakasu
label: Nakasu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '福博であい橋' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '福博であい橋' (relation/10159847): middle (92 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19383249: large area 'Nakasu' (956 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Island entertainment district with riverside yatai food stalls and neon lights.

text.description:
Nakasu is a narrow island in the middle of Fukuoka, lying between the Naka River and the Hakata River. Its name means roughly "the island in the middle". It was created around 1600 by Kuroda Nagamasa, the local lord, who joined the two sides of the city with bridges, and today the island has 18 bridges. It is now a busy entertainment district. Its restaurants and shops are said to number about 3,500, and more than 60,000 people reportedly pass through on an average night.

It photographs best after dark, when neon signs and the yatai (food stall) lights spill onto the water. The classic picture is taken from the Fukuhaku Deai Bridge (福博であい橋), where the bridge's own lighting frames Nakasu's glow and the lights reflect in the Naka River. Reflections are the point of the shot, so look for a calm stretch of water and let the lit-up riverbank fill the upper half of the frame.

If you want something wider, the Nishi-ōhashi bridge (西大橋) gives a broad view of the built-up island and the river running alongside it. The bridge lighting is seasonal, so check the dates before you plan an evening around it.

The streets are lively at night. Take your time on the bridge and keep out of the way of people walking past.
text.geographic_location: Nakasu is the island between the Naka River and the Hakata River in central Fukuoka, joining Chūō-ku and Hakata-ku. It lies next to the Sumiyoshi district, where Canal City Hakata is.
text.directions_text: The nearest subway station to Nakasu is Nakasu-Kawabata Station on the Fukuoka City Subway. From the station, walk to the Fukuhaku Deai Bridge, a known viewpoint for Nakasu's neon signs and the Naka River. From the bridge, the centre of Nakasu is to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge, the river and the reflections. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the lit-up riverbank, but keep the horizon level so the buildings don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 福博であい橋. Nakasu's neon and yatai lights reflecting on the Naka River, framed by the illuminated bridge. From there you look across the Naka River to Nakasu's neon and yatai lights reflected in the water, with the bridge's own lighting framing the view. Nakasu's main area lies to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the reflections fill the lower part of the frame and the lit buildings sit above them. Include a little of the bridge's lit edge to give the picture depth. For a wider view of the island, Nishi-ōhashi bridge is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode and brace your elbows on the railing or hold your breath as it takes the shot, so the reflections stay sharp. Tap on a bright sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the neon doesn't wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the lights are on. The bridge illuminations are seasonal, with a winter period of roughly November 2026 to January 2027, so check before you go.

text.access_note: The bridge is an open public crossing, but check the official site before you go for the dates of the seasonal lighting.

name: Acros Fukuoka
label: Acros Fukuoka
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '天神中央公園' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '天神中央公園' (way/33111543): middle (253 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N9218958236 (Acros Fukuoka and In front of Suikyō Tenmangu Shrine): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Stepped garden building covered in greenery next to Tenjin Central Park.

text.description:
Acros Fukuoka is a large building in the Tenjin area whose front is built as a series of green terraces, so from the right angle it looks less like an office block and more like a tree-covered hill rising out of the city. That is the main reason it photographs well. The planted steps give you texture and colour, and the open lawn in front gives you room to stand back and take it all in.

The classic view is from Tenjin Central Park, directly in front of the building. From the south side of the park you look north across the lawn and trees to the whole stepped, planted facade, with sky above it. Trees and lawn in the foreground add depth, and they stop the picture being just a wall of building. If you want something closer, the building itself offers close-up shots of its cascading planters and vines, with the glass atrium or the city visible through the greenery. Suijō Park is a possible alternative for a side-on view with Tenjin's streets and trees in front.

Keep your phone level so the terraces don't lean, and let some lawn or trees into the bottom of the frame. If you plan to go up the building or into the garden, access arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Acros Fukuoka is in the Tenjin district of central Fukuoka, facing Tenjin Central Park on the park's north side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Tenjin area of Fukuoka and then walk to Tenjin Central Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand to get the stepped facade, lawn and sky in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit the whole building in, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the planters and vines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 天神中央公園 (south side, facing north across the lawn toward the building). The whole stepped, tree-covered facade of the building rising over the park's lawn and trees, with the sky above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's horizontal terraces with them so the picture looks straight. Include a strip of lawn and some trees at the bottom for depth. For a different shot, go closer to the building for the cascading planters and vines, or try Suijō Park for a side-on view with Tenjin's streets in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the green facade to set focus and exposure, then nudge the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Take a few frames at 0.5x, 1x and a zoomed setting so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, when the planting looks green and the terraces show clearly. A clear sky behind the building helps the outline stand out.

text.access_note: The park is a public open space with no entry charge, but the building's garden and observation areas may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka
label: PayPay Dome
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'シーサイドももち海浜公園' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'シーサイドももち海浜公園' (way/900420523): edge nearest the subject (1125 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28445837: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'MIZUHO PayPay Dome FUKUOKA' (306 m across).
notes: Retractable-roof baseball stadium of the SoftBank Hawks.

text.description:
The Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka is the home ground of the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks baseball team, in Chūō-ku, close to Momochi Beach. It opened in 1993 with about 40,000 seats, and it was Japan's first stadium with a retractable roof. The roof is a huge steel structure of around 12,000 tonnes covered in thin titanium plating, which gives the building its smooth, curved, silvery look. The roof is rarely opened, so you will most likely see it closed.

The best way to photograph it is from the beach side, where the dome has room to breathe. The sand and sea in the foreground make the picture feel like a seaside scene rather than a stadium shot.

Keep the horizon level and let the sand or promenade fill the lower third of the frame. People walking along the promenade add scale. If you want a close, head-on view of the building, the wide front staircase (ドーム前大階段) gives a frontal view of the facade that fills the frame. Only the outside is on offer on days without events, so treat this as an exterior photo stop.
text.geographic_location: The dome is in Chūō-ku, in the Momochi waterfront area of Fukuoka, next to Momochi Beach and Hakata Bay. The beach-side viewpoint is on the seaward, western side of the dome.
text.directions_text: The dome is about a 15 minute walk from Tōjinmachi Station on the Fukuoka City Subway. If you would rather not walk, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Momochi Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole roof, the beach and the bay. Then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer view, and 2x or more if your phone has telephoto to make the dome look bigger behind the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in シーサイドももち海浜公園 (beach side of the park, facing the dome across the sand). The dome's curved titanium roof rising behind the beach and promenade, framed by the open waterfront of Hakata Bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the roof sits in the middle of the frame, with sand or promenade below. Keep the phone level so the roof's curve looks natural and the sea edge stays straight. For a different angle, the wide front staircase (ドーム前大階段) shows the facade head-on, filling the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale roof keeps its detail. If a wide shot of the whole waterfront appeals, panorama mode works well along the beach, but hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is behind you in the west, should light the side of the dome facing the beach. Around dusk, night mode helps with the glowing sky and lights, but hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.

text.access_note: The beach side of the park is open public space, but the dome is only photographed from outside; exterior access can change on game and event days, so check the official site and the Hawks schedule before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: In late afternoon the sun is in the west, behind someone standing west of the dome, so it should light the dome's beach-facing side.
The roof will most likely be closed when visitors arrive, because the sources say it is rarely opened.
The walking time of about 6 to 7 minutes is estimated from the roughly 500 m distance on the map, not from a source.
A taxi or hired scooter is a possible way to reach Momochi Beach for those who do not want to walk from Tōjinmachi Station.
Panorama mode and night mode are suggested for the waterfront and dusk scenes.

name: Shōfuku-ji
label: Shofukuji Temple
camera_source: Commons cluster (2 photos), weak. Moved 140 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 130 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/767775376: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shōfuku-ji Temple' (344 m across).
notes: Japan's oldest Zen temple, founded in 1195.

text.description: Shōfuku-ji is a Zen Buddhist temple in the Hakata part of Fukuoka, and it is described as the oldest Zen temple in Japan. It was founded by the monk Eisai, who returned from China in 1195, and the main buildings went up in the early 1200s. Its grounds are a protected National Historic Site. For a visitor with a phone, the appeal is calm and simple: timber gates, old tiled roofs and tall trees in the middle of a busy city. Some of the buildings have travelled. According to temple legend, the Sanmon gate came from Najima Castle, and the Hōjō hall was moved from Hizen Nagoya Castle in 1601. The bell tower dates from 1589. The temple precinct is large, about 344 m across on the map, so you will want to choose a few views rather than try to fit it all in. Gates make good frames. Stand square on, keep the roofline level, and let a path or the trees lead the eye towards the buildings. Look for the small details too: roof tiles, wooden beams and the bell tower. The grounds also include a cemetery, so keep voices down, photograph the buildings rather than the graves, and stay out of anyone's way.
text.geographic_location: Shōfuku-ji is in the Gokushōmachi neighbourhood of Hakata, in central Fukuoka, a short walk from Gion Station.
text.directions_text: No tram stop is listed for this spot. Gion Station on the Fukuoka City Subway Airport Line is about a three-minute walk from the temple. The temple's centre lies 129 m to the north of it, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for gates and building fronts. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the larger open spaces. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details, carved beams and the bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the gate, looking up at it from the approach path). The large two-storey wooden gate framing the temple, shot head-on from the approach, with blossoms in the foreground in spring if you want a softer frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate or hall with the vertical lines, so the roof sits level. Use the paths and trees as frames. For a tighter shot, zoom in on a single roofline against the sky instead of trying to fit in the whole building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so that pale sky does not wash out the dark timber. If the grounds are shady, hold the phone steady with both hands and brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day, when the grounds are quieter and the light is softer, is likely to give the cleanest shots with fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple with historic grounds; check the official site before you go for what is open and what may be photographed.
claims_not_in_sources: The temple grounds are likely to be quieter and the light softer earlier in the day.
Visitors should keep quiet and avoid photographing the graves in the cemetery.
Some buildings or areas may be closed to visitors or have photography restrictions.

name: Fukuoka Asian Art Museum
label: Asian Art Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1423779941: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fukuoka Asian Art Museum'.
notes: Museum of modern Asian art in the Hakata Riverain building.

text.description:
Fukuoka Asian Art Museum is a gallery of modern and contemporary Asian art in the Hakata part of Fukuoka. It opened in 1999. The collection holds about three thousand works from twenty-three countries, and most of it came to the museum through donations and gifts. The museum grew out of the earlier Fukuoka Art Museum, which put on an Asian art show every five years from 1979 to 1994, at a time when contemporary Asian art attracted little interest.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the setting and the story. A quick shot of the entrance or signage makes a good record of the visit, and it sits well in a set of photos of the city. Take a wide view first to show where you are, then a closer one of any signs, banners or posters that name the museum. Keep your phone upright for a tall frontage and sideways for a wider scene.

If you go inside, rules on photography can differ from one gallery or exhibition to the next. Look for signs, or ask staff, before you take pictures of the artworks. Keep the phone steady and quiet, and don't use flash. Check the official site before you go for the latest visiting details.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Hakata district of Fukuoka, in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Hakata area of Fukuoka and head for the phone icon on the map. Once you can see the museum name on the map, follow it on foot for the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the entrance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the building in. Use 2x or more only for details such as signs or banners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back as far as is comfortable and safe to fit more of the frontage into your shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with them so the walls look straight. Keep any signage in the top or bottom third of the picture. For a second shot, move in close on a poster, banner or sign with the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building on screen to focus, then slide the exposure control down a little if the sky is bright. Indoors, switch off the flash and hold the phone steady with both hands. Use night mode only if the light is low.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in soft, even light works best for outside shots, because there are fewer harsh shadows on the front of the building.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for visiting details and any rules on photography inside the galleries.

name: Hakata Port Tower
label: Hakata Port Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '博多ポートタワー' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/684600217: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hakata Port Tower' (49 m across).
notes: Harbour observation tower with a diamond-like glass facade.

text.description:
Hakata Port Tower is a slim lattice tower on the Hakata waterfront in Fukuoka. It is 103 metres tall and was built in 1964, and its observation deck sits at 73.5 metres. The open-framed structure is easy to pick out against sea and sky, which makes it a tidy subject for a phone photo. The waterfront and the outdoor deck beside it give you space to step back and include the harbour, so the picture says 'Fukuoka port' rather than just 'tall tower'.

Because the tower is so tall, you will not fit all of it into the frame when standing close. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and tilt the phone upwards, or step back along the waterfront and use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more even view. Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. If a second angle appeals, the Hakata Port waterfront (博多埠頭) shows the tower rising above the harbour, with the water in the foreground.

Guides suggest late afternoon into sunset, when the tower's night lighting begins. That gives you a softer sky and the lit tower in one go. If you want a higher view, the tower has an observation deck, but opening times and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Hakata Port Tower is in Hakata-ku, Fukuoka, on the Hakata harbour waterfront.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Hakata Port waterfront in Hakata-ku, Fukuoka. The tower is tall and easy to spot as you approach. The phone icon on the map sits at the tower itself, so once you arrive, step back along the waterfront to frame it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close, to fit more of the tower in. Switch to the default lens (1x) when you stand further back on the waterfront. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the top of the tower or the observation level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The waterfront and outdoor deck beside the tower are the practical places to stand and shoot. Step back along the waterfront or deck until the tower fits the frame, so you are shooting the tower against the harbour waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line to keep it straight. Leave some water or waterfront at the bottom of the frame for context. If you want a different view, the Hakata Port waterfront (博多埠頭) shows the tower rising above the harbour, with the water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the sky keeps its colour. Once the tower lights come on, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, when the tower's night lighting begins.

text.access_note: The waterfront is the place to photograph the tower from outside, but the tower's observation deck may have set opening times and entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hakozaki Shrine
label: Hakozaki Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '一之鳥居' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '筥崎宮本殿' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10406513: large area 'Hakozaki Shrine' (1077 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: One of Japan's three great Hachiman shrines, with a large tower gate.

text.description: Hakozaki Shrine is one of Fukuoka's most important Shintō shrines, dedicated to the kami Hachiman. It was founded in 923, and it was burned down during the Mongol invasion of 1274. When it was rebuilt, the tower gate was given a calligraphy panel reading Tekikoku kōfuku, meaning 'surrender of the enemy nation'. The main hall, the worship hall and the tower gate are all listed as important cultural assets of Japan. It photographs well because the long approach lines up the gate and the main hall, so one frame can show the whole sequence. The first torii gate that once stood here was taken down in 2018 and has not been replaced, so expect an open approach rather than a gate framing the view. Take the photo from the approach itself and keep the tower gate and main hall in the middle third of the frame. Photography inside the main hall and during ceremonies is restricted, and drones and commercial shoots are not allowed on the grounds. Festival days, such as the Tamaseseri Festival on 3 January and the Hojoya Festival from 12 to 18 September, bring many visitors, so allow extra time then.
text.geographic_location: Hakozaki Shrine is in the Hakozaki area of Fukuoka, on the coastal side of the city. The grounds run down to the white-sand beach called お潮井浜.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The shrine is about 28 m to the south-west, which is under a minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the approach, tower gate and main hall together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if crowds or a close position stop you fitting the scene in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower gate or its roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (stand on the approach, facing the tower gate and main hall). The shrine's torii gate, tower gate and main hall framed together in one frame. The torii that once stood here was removed in 2018, so check what you can see on arrival.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower gate on the central line, keeping the approach as a leading line toward it. Hold the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a different shot, the beach お潮井浜 shows the shrine grounds across the white sand. The long vermilion fence around the main hall makes a strong backdrop for portraits.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich. Use portrait mode for people against the fence. Please do not photograph inside the main hall or during ceremonies.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer and gives softer light. Avoid the festival days (3 January and 12 to 18 September) if you want clear views of the approach.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, with some photography restrictions and a ban on drones and commercial shoots, so check the official site before you go.

name: Jōten-ji
label: Joten-ji Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '承天寺通り' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '承天寺通り' (way/169674157): point nearest the subject (344 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5786025954: the OpenStreetMap point 'Jyoten-ji Temple'.
notes: Temple in Hakata old town, tied to the origins of udon and soba in Japan.

text.description: Jōten-ji is a Rinzai Zen temple in the Hakata part of Fukuoka. The priest Enni-Ben'en founded it after returning from China, and building work was completed in 1242. He is also credited with bringing the know-how for udon, soba and manjū back to Japan, so the temple is a nice stop for anyone curious about the city's food history. Looking north along the lane, you can see the temple's traditional buildings and the white-gravel sand garden at a distance, with trees framing the scene. The stone paving and greenery make a good foreground, so you don't need to go inside to get a satisfying picture. Near the start of the lane stands the Hakata Sennen Gate, finished on 28 March 2014. It is a wooden four-legged gate with a tile roof, about 8 metres tall and wide, modelled on an old gateway of Hakata. Its roof tiles carry peach-shaped ornaments, and the path continues behind it, which makes a good second shot. Keep the lane in the lower third of the frame and let the temple roofs and trees fill the rest. Some areas of the temple are restricted for photography, so follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: Jōten-ji is in the Hakata district of Fukuoka, on Jōtenji-dori Avenue. The Hakata Sennen Gate marks the entrance to the avenue.
text.directions_text: Jōten-ji is in the Hakata area of Fukuoka, on Jōtenji-dori Avenue, near the Hakata Sennen Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane, temple and trees together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane feels too narrow to fit the stone paving and the roofs. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the gravel garden and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 承天寺通り (stone-paved lane beside the temple, viewed from the street). The temple's traditional buildings and its white-gravel sand garden seen over the stone-paved lane, framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stone paving along the bottom of the frame so it leads the eye towards the temple. Keep the trees on one side as a natural border. For a second picture, walk to the Hakata Sennen Gate (博多千年門) and photograph its peach-ornamented roof tiles with the approach path behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the white gravel looks washed out. At night, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be calmer. In the evening the grounds can get busy during the Hakata light-up walk, so be patient and wait for gaps in the crowd.

text.access_note: The lane is a public street, but the temple grounds and the sand garden inside may be ticketed and some areas restrict photography, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is likely to be quieter than later on.
The 0.5x ultra-wide lens helps fit more of a narrow lane into the frame.
White gravel can look overexposed on a phone, so lowering the exposure slider may help.
